title: India Moves OCI Applications Fully Online Under New Citizenship Rules
excerpt: The Citizenship (Amendment) Rules, 2026, mandate electronic filing for all OCI services, introduce digital e-OCI cards, and bar minors from holding dual passports.
body:
• India's Ministry of Home Affairs has notified the Citizenship (Amendment) Rules, 2026, requiring all OCI registration, renunciation, and cancellation requests to be filed electronically through ociservices.gov.in.
  • The rules introduce electronic OCI (e-OCI) cards as an alternative to physical cards, with all records now maintained digitally by issuing authorities.
  • Minors holding Indian passports are barred from simultaneously holding a foreign passport, and OCI applicants must consent to biometric collection for the Fast Track Immigration Programme.
  • A new USD 25 fine applies to OCI holders who fail to update passport details on the portal within three months of receiving a new passport.

A Digital Overhaul for Millions of OCI Holders

India has overhauled its Overseas Citizen of India framework, shifting the entire system from paper-based processing to a centralized digital platform. The Citizenship (Amendment) Rules, 2026, published in the official gazette on April 30, amend the Citizenship Rules, 2009, and take effect immediately, according to the Ministry of Home Affairs notification.

The changes represent the most significant update to the OCI program since its introduction in 2005. Every OCI application — whether for registration, re-issuance, renunciation, or cancellation — must now be submitted electronically through the designated portal at ociservices.gov.in, according to Livemint. The previous requirement of submitting documents in duplicate has been eliminated entirely.

E-OCI: A Digital Card for a Digital Age

Perhaps the most consequential change is the introduction of electronic OCI (e-OCI) registration. Under the revised Rule 33, registered OCI cardholders will receive either a physical OCI card or an e-OCI registration, both documented in the updated Form XXIX. Issuing authorities are now required to maintain all OCI records in electronic form, replacing the earlier system of monthly paper forwarding to the Ministry of Home Affairs.

"The e-OCI changes this by allowing OCI status to exist purely as a digital record in a government register."

— RPV Legal, Mondaq analysis

According to immigration consultancy Fragomen, the e-OCI is linked to upgraded biometric verification systems that will support faster "e-gate" immigration processing at Indian airports through real-time matching of passport and OCI data. Processing times are expected to decrease from the current six to eight weeks to approximately 15 working days, with biometric-enabled e-gates operational at 13 international airports.

Dual Passport Ban for Minors and New Compliance Rules

The rules clarify a long-standing area of confusion around minor children. A new proviso to Rule 3 states that "the minor child cannot at any time hold the passport of any other country while also holding the Indian passport." Previously, a parent could register a child's birth at an Indian consulate and later obtain a foreign passport without any recorded acknowledgment that this was inconsistent with Indian citizenship, according to an analysis by RPV Legal published on Mondaq.

For existing OCI holders, the rules introduce a new compliance requirement: a USD 25 fine for those who fail to update their passport details on the OCI portal within three months of receiving a new passport, according to Fragomen. This adds a time-bound obligation that did not previously exist.

Biometric Consent and Broader Eligibility

The revised application form (Form XXVIII) includes a mandatory consent clause requiring applicants to agree to share biometric information collected during OCI registration for future enrollment in the Fast Track Immigration Programme. There is no option to withhold consent — biometric data sharing is effectively a condition of OCI registration.

The rules also expand eligibility in two areas. Eligible foreign nationals can now apply for an OCI card without completing the previously required six months of stay in India, provided they hold a valid long-term visa and necessary documents. Additionally, fifth- and sixth-generation Indian-origin Tamils in Sri Lanka are now eligible, extending the previous limit of fourth-generation descendants, according to Fragomen.

What This Means for the Diaspora

For the estimated 4 million OCI cardholders worldwide, the transition to digital-first processing is a double-edged sword. The elimination of paper-based applications and duplicate document submissions should reduce bureaucratic friction and processing delays. Real-time tracking of applications will replace the opaque waiting periods that have long frustrated applicants at Indian consulates abroad.

However, the mandatory biometric consent clause and the new passport-update fine introduce compliance obligations that require active monitoring. OCI holders who renew their passports will need to update the portal within 90 days or face penalties. Those holding physical OCI cards who wish to renounce must still physically surrender their cards to the nearest Indian Mission or FRRO, even as the declaration itself moves online.

Revised Appeals Process

The rules also restructure how applicants can challenge adverse decisions. For OCI-specific decisions made by Indian Missions, Posts, or Foreigners Regional Registration Officers, the Central Government will now designate a specific review authority rather than relying on the previous "one rank higher" principle, which often created confusion at overseas posts, according to the Livemint report. A right to be heard is now expressly written into the rules for both revision and review proceedings under Section 15A.

What's Next

The rules are already in effect, with ociservices.gov.in serving as the sole gateway for all OCI transactions. Immigration attorneys are advising OCI holders to verify their portal accounts and ensure passport details are current to avoid the new penalties. The transition period is expected to bring some turbulence as consulates adjust their operations, but the long-term direction is unmistakable: India's OCI system is going paperless.
